changes.rationale: The newly supplied complete 99-page public preprint is directly linked to mutable public OSF project 2egqr by the saved node/folder/file metadata and identity receipt; no identity with the different qswe3/u59ab thesis is assumed. Having independently read all 166,079 characters of the main report and supplementary, I agree with the fresh sanitized proposal on the outcome, using it only as a proposal. The abstract explicitly states that the authors successfully replicated and extended Experiments 1A and 2 to 4 of Young and Saxe (2011). This is a genuine overall verdict about the named replication set, rather than confirmation of just one effect. Under codebook rule 1 that verdict governs the single original-paper outcome. The discussion also says all original significant effects were successfully replicated. The strongest alternative is mixed: results give partial support for adjusted hypotheses 2 and 3, and the discussion/conclusion explicitly contrast emotion and disgust specificity with the original. Those are real original-specific countercomparisons, not extension-only or irrelevant analyses, and would support mixed under rule 2 absent the overall verdict. Nevertheless the later synthesis describes strong and weak support and non-specificity without retracting the set-wide successful verdict or declaring the replication overall partial/mixed. Thus it qualifies the successful verdict rather than superseding it. Experiment 2's adjusted comparison is included by the abstract, even though the all-significant-effects summary alone would not settle its original null findings. Smaller effects and signal-inconsistent labels alone do not make mixed. Moral responsibility is an expressly separate extension and its support or contrast with Parkinson and Byrne does not decide this Young/Saxe outcome. The old cached text genuinely contains explicit randomized-data warnings and an unfinished Stage 2 discussion, so its cannot_be_determined judgment remains a valid source-bound prior opinion. Those warnings do not describe this new completed report, which states completed collection, supplies actual main results and a substantive discussion, and documents pre/post-exclusion results and a corrected emotion-rating coding deviation. Residual supplementary templates do not negate these results; authors do not give an uninformative or statistically-successful-but-flawed verdict. The old claim that no completed report linked to 2egqr is available is now superseded by this new evidence; no outcome is transferred from another record. Only row 2388 outcome is proposed for correction, from shipped mixed/current cannot_be_determined to successful.

changes.rationale: Approve successful narrowly for agreement with Camerer (2018)'s Shah Study 1 finding, under codebook Step 3 rule 2 and its explicit original-null rule. The chain target remains Camerer, not Shah. The full original article and relevant SM now establish what that target found: Shah Study 1 failed in Camerer, with pooled r = −0.015, p = 0.710, N = 619 (SM Table 4), and the article treats the eight statistical failures as the eight default-Bayes-factor results supporting the null. Table 4 places Shah in that set; the original author's own failed Study 1 replication is explicitly described as consistent with/confirming Camerer's finding. This is substantive original-null evidence beyond a pair of nonsignificant p values. The current report retests the same poor-versus-rich Dots-Mixed comparison using Camerer's exact materials and reports a near-zero nonsignificant result, F(1,666) = .99, p = .319; its own discussion characterizes minimal cognitive influence. Thus both implicit-comparison tests pass: the original finding is established and the corresponding current result is identifiable. The current explicit failure verdict names Shah's positive finding; it is not an overall failure verdict against Camerer's null finding. The stated difference in sample-mean direction is retained, but neither report establishes a reverse substantive effect: Camerer's own signed estimate is near zero and its inferential interpretation supports absence of the positive scarcity effect. That sample-sign contrast is not a second tested finding that disagrees with Camerer's substantive conclusion, so it does not require mixed. Current authors decline to accept an exact null; this limits evidentiary strength and prevents an equivalence claim, but does not erase their directly corresponding result under the codebook. No overall Camerer-specific verdict overrides this implicit comparison. Approval concerns this one assigned comparison only, with no original-identity, type, removal, other-target or canonical change.

proofs.quote: We observed that low-wealth subjects given fewer chances to win in repeated “Wheel of Fortune” type word puzzle games, performed worse on the Dots-Mixed attention task (M = 41.56, SD = 16.79) than high-wealth individuals (M = 42.82, SD = 15.87), however, this result was not statistically significant (F(1,666) = .99, p=.319). This result did not replicate the findings from Study 1 of Shah et al. (2012), but the means were not in the opposite direction of their results as seen in Camerer et al. (2018).

changes.rationale: The shipped mixed outcome is not supported for the Berinsky, Huber, and Lenz (2012) experimental findings. The abstract explicitly says that the same analyses are replicated; Figure 2's introductory text compares Lucid, MTurk and original experimental estimates; Experiments 1–4 report shared findings rather than merely citing a method. Most decisively, Experiment 3 states the risk-acceptance finding and that it replicated in both MTurk and Lucid, and Note 10 explicitly identifies Berinsky et al. (2012) as the report of that earlier replication. These are new-sample retests of the earlier replication's reported empirical finding, permissible under the closest-actually-retested chain rule. Calling the paper a methodological template or naming its older source does not negate this relationship. The current source reports the same qualitative risky-choice conclusions across all three samples, agreement for welfare wording, and similar experimental estimates for free trade. For free trade, the sentence about the combined frame names original and MTurk only; it does not state a Lucid disagreement, while the authors explicitly judge the studies similar. No overall verdict specifically on the 2012 target supersedes these comparisons; applying outcome rule 2 to the shared experimental findings supports successful. The discussion's sole substantively different experiment is explicitly Berinsky (2017), and the main text says that experiment has no prior MTurk replication. Its healthcare-rumor divergence must not be inherited by the 2012 target. The outcome correction is conditional on parent resolution of the original-row dependency: the evidence supports retaining the earlier-replication target, whereas unconditional not_applicable/removal is not supported by the prior template-only rationale. Parent owns any original-field change, closest-chain reconciliation and duplicate removal across sibling targets; this result assigns only outcome. No claim of report equivalence or distinctness rests on DOI/year alone.

proofs.quote:
Our point of departure is the 2012 study by Berinsky, Huber, and Lenz that compares
Amazon’s Mechanical Turk to US national probability samples in terms of respondent characteristics and treatment
effect estimates. We replicate these same analyses using a large sample of survey responses on the Lucid platform.

In the Welfare,
Asian Disease, Kam and Simas, Hiscox and Berinsky facets found in Figure 2, we present standardized treatment
effect estimates, where we have scaled the outcome variables for Lucid and MTurk by the mean and standard deviation of the original experiments. The Berinsky facet does
not include an MTurk estimate since it has not been previously replicated on an MTurk sample.

This experiment behaves on Lucid
much as it does on MTurk and the GSS – a large increase in
support for redistribution when the question is phrased as
assistance or caring for the poor rather than as “welfare.”

Across all three samples (the original experiment was
conducted in a classroom setting among undergraduates),
the treatment has average effects in the same direction,
with subjects in the mortality (loss) frame far more likely
to choose the probabilistic (risky) outcome, though the
magnitudes of the effects do differ substantially by

show that risk acceptance correlates with choosing the risky
option in an Asian Disease-type experiment, but that the

both MTurk and Lucid samples. Receiving the mortality

The Expert frame increases support
for free trade in all examined samples, while the positive
frame has negligible (or even negative) effects and the negative frame has unambiguously negative effects. In both the
original sample and the MTurk sample, the combination of

10. Berinsky et al. (2012) analyze the original and their replication using a probit model, but we use ordinary least
squares (OLS). While some analysts prefer to use nonlinear models like logit or probit when the dependent variable
is binary, in an experiment, OLS (without adjustment) is
unbiased for the ATE (or, as in this case, the CATEs). See
Gerber and Green (2012: ch. 2) for a textbook proof. The
substantive conclusions do not change in any way if we use
probit regression.

We conclude our set of five experiments with a note of caution. We attempted to replicate Berinsky’s 2017 experiment
on belief in rumors surrounding the Affordable Care Act
(ACA), specifically the false rumor that the ACA would
create “death panels” that would make end-of-life decisions
for patients without their consent. In the original experiment (conducted in 2010 on a sample provided by Survey
Sampling International (SSI)), a large portion of the sample
believed the rumor, and corrections delivered by
Republicans, Democrats, and Nonpartisan groups were all
effective in correcting false beliefs.

Among our five experiments, we have one instance of
the Lucid sample producing substantively different
results compared to the original study. In no way do we
think our results contradict or overturn those reported by
Berinsky (2017).
